prompt: With tcp dport { 80, 443 } allowed, laptop reached an SSH server on remote. Why did the rule let it through?
hint: What did the rule ask about?

choices.text: SSH is encrypted, so the firewall could not see the port
choices.why: The port is in the TCP header, which is never encrypted by SSH.

choices.text: It listened on 443
choices.why: Right. The rule asked about the port and nothing else.

choices.text: Port 22 was open as well, and SSH fell back to it
choices.why: Port 22 was closed; nc to it failed with exit 1.

choices.text: ct state established matched the first packet
choices.why: The first packet is new; the 443 rule accepted it.

prompt: Which of these does tcp dport 443 accept? Choose all that apply.
hint: The rule reads one number.

choices.text: A browser fetching a page over HTTPS
choices.why: That is what it was written for.

choices.text: An SSH session to a server listening on 443
choices.why: The lesson ran exactly this.

choices.text: Remote-control software calling home on 443
choices.why: It picks 443 because every network leaves it open.

choices.text: A DNS query to port 53
choices.why: Different port, and UDP.

prompt: Who decides which protocol travels on port 443?
hint: Think about who picks each end.

choices.text: IANA, which assigns the port numbers and enforces them
choices.why: IANA lists conventions; nothing enforces them on the wire.

choices.text: The firewall, which checks the protocol of every port
choices.why: A header rule checks no protocol at all.

choices.text: The two programs, by agreeing on it
choices.why: Right. The server listens there and the client asks there.

choices.text: The operating system, which binds 443 to TLS
choices.why: Any program may listen on 443 given the privilege.

prompt: Match each protocol to how its conversation opens.
hint: The parsers look at the first bytes.

pairs.right: a method, a path and HTTP/1.1

right_distractors: a port number in the TCP header

prompt: Suricata named the flow to app on port 8080 http. What did it base that on?
hint: 8080 is not HTTP's registered port.

choices.text: The port, since 8080 is a well-known alternative for HTTP
choices.why: It would have named it http on any port.

choices.text: The first bytes of the conversation
choices.why: Right: GET / HTTP/1.1.

choices.text: A DNS lookup of app's name
choices.why: The request used an address.

choices.text: The rule file, which listed 8080 as HTTP
choices.why: The rule file was empty.

prompt: A vendor says its NGFW blocks SSH on any port. When does the block take effect on a new SSH connection to port 443?
hint: There has to be something to read.

choices.text: Before the TCP handshake, from the SYN
choices.why: A SYN carries no payload to identify.

choices.text: Only when the session ends, from the flow record
choices.why: Inline inspection acts during the flow.

choices.text: After the first bytes, once the greeting is seen
choices.why: Right. The first packets pass on the port rule.

choices.text: Never, because SSH is encrypted end to end
choices.why: The greeting is plain text and identifies SSH.

prompt: Reading the payload as well as the headers is called deep packet ___.
hint: The lesson's title says it.

prompt: Match each part of the Suricata rule to what it says.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.right: what to do on a match
the protocol as recognised, on any port
the client's side of a completed handshake

prompt: The rule for TLS on a port other than 443 produced no alert. What does that tell you?
hint: Where did this capture's TLS go?

choices.text: The rule failed to load
choices.why: suricata -T loaded the configuration successfully.

choices.text: No TLS in the capture went anywhere but 443
choices.why: Right. A good policy rule is silent most of the time.

choices.text: Suricata cannot recognise TLS outside port 443
choices.why: It named HTTP on 8080; it recognises TLS the same way.

choices.text: The SNI was encrypted, so the content check had nothing
choices.why: The SNI was read: www.example.com.

prompt: An NGFW has an application rule denying SSH. Why does it still need port rules underneath?
hint: Which is cheaper, and which comes first?

choices.text: They decide what opens at all, before the slower inspection
choices.why: Right. An application rule narrows a port rule; it does not replace it.

choices.text: Application rules only work on standard ports
choices.why: The lesson recognised SSH on 443 and HTTP on 8080.

choices.text: Port rules log more detail than application rules
choices.why: They see less, not more.

choices.text: The law requires a port-based rule set on every edge
choices.why: No such law; it is a matter of cost and order.

prompt: Local rules in this lesson take sid numbers from what value upwards?
hint: A million.

prompt: From the TLS 1.3 connection to www, what did Suricata read?
hint: Look at which fields were not null.

choices.text: The path and the response code
choices.why: Those are inside the encryption.

choices.text: The certificate's subject and issuer
choices.why: Both null: TLS 1.3 encrypts the certificate.

choices.text: The user agent of the client
choices.why: That is an HTTP header, encrypted here.

choices.text: The server name and the version
choices.why: Right: the SNI and TLS 1.3.

prompt: Against TLS it cannot decrypt, what can an inspector still decide on? Choose all that apply.
hint: Metadata.

choices.text: The server name in the SNI
choices.why: Sent in clear in the first message.

choices.text: Which protocol the flow carries
choices.why: Recognised from the handshake.

choices.text: How much traffic and how often
choices.why: Counted from the packets.

choices.text: The words of a message sent through it
choices.why: That is exactly what encryption hides.

prompt: A company turns on TLS inspection. Which new risk is the firewall itself now carrying?
hint: What does it hold in clear?

choices.text: Its throughput doubles and overloads the switches
choices.why: Inspection lowers throughput.

choices.text: It holds everyone's traffic in clear, so it is the prize
choices.why: Right. Compromise it and you read everything.

choices.text: Browsers stop trusting the public authorities
choices.why: They trust one more authority; the others stay.

choices.text: It can no longer see the SNI
choices.why: It sees more than before, not less.

prompt: Why does TLS inspection break a program that checks a client certificate?
hint: Two connections, and whose keys are on each.

choices.text: Client certificates are not supported by TLS 1.3
choices.why: They are part of TLS 1.3.

choices.text: The firewall strips every certificate from the handshake
choices.why: It replaces the server's, it does not strip.

choices.text: The firewall cannot present the client's private key
choices.why: Right. The key never leaves the client.

choices.text: The server sees the firewall's address
choices.why: Addresses are not what a client certificate proves.

prompt: Match each NGFW feature to what it does.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.right: ties an address to a signed-in person
drops traffic matching a known signature
allows or blocks by the site's category
runs downloads somewhere safe to watch them

prompt: A firewall is sized by its headline throughput, then every inspection feature is turned on. What happens?
hint: Vendors quote two numbers.

choices.text: Nothing: inspection is done in the same hardware at no cost
choices.why: Payload reading is software work per packet.

choices.text: It forwards far less than the headline figure
choices.why: Right. The inspection figure is the one that applies.

choices.text: The firewall disables stateful tracking to compensate
choices.why: Nothing is traded away automatically.

choices.text: Encrypted traffic is dropped
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson drops it.

prompt: Where is an NGFW the wrong tool?
hint: Volume, and trust between the machines.

choices.text: At the internet edge
choices.why: That is its natural place.

choices.text: Between the staff LAN and the servers
choices.why: A boundary between zones of different trust suits it.

choices.text: Deep in a data centre, between machines that trust each other and move the most traffic
choices.why: Right. Lesson 21 uses rules on the machines there.

choices.text: In front of the DMZ
choices.why: Another boundary, and a good place.

prompt: A policy says staff may not upload files to storage services the company has not approved. Which layer can enforce it for HTTPS traffic without decrypting?
hint: What is visible in a TLS 1.3 ClientHello?

choices.text: A port rule allowing only 443
choices.why: Every such service uses 443.

choices.text: A rule on the SNI's server name
choices.why: Right. The name is in clear; the file contents are not.

choices.text: A rule matching the uploaded file's contents
choices.why: The contents are encrypted.

choices.text: A stateful rule on established traffic
choices.why: That allows every conversation already started.

prompt: Order the layers a packet from the internet meets, from cheapest to most expensive.
hint: Lesson 1 and this lesson.
items: a stateless filter at the border
trap: Each layer reads more and so costs more; the cheap ones throw away what the expensive ones never need to see.

prompt: Only the port rule set is loaded on fw. Which question can it answer?
hint: Headers only.

choices.text: Is this flow on 443 really HTTPS?
choices.why: That needs the payload.

choices.text: Which employee opened this connection?
choices.why: That needs user identity.

choices.text: What page was requested over TLS?
choices.why: That needs decryption.

choices.text: Did this start on the LAN?
choices.why: Right: the interface and the state are header facts.
